  - Draft a concise (1-2 sentences) commit message that focuses on the "why" rather than the "what"
  - Ensure it accurately reflects the changes and their purpose
3. Run the following commands in parallel:
   - Add relevant untracked files to the staging area.
   - Create the commit with a message, ending with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.
   - Run git status after the commit completes to verify success.
   Note: git status depends on the commit completing, so run it sequentially after the commit.

- NEVER run additional commands to read or explore code, besides git bash commands
- NEVER use the TaskCreate or Agent tools
- DO NOT push to the remote repository unless the user explicitly asks you to do so

- In order to ensure good formatting, ALWAYS pass the commit message via a HEREDOC, a la this example:

   EOF
   )"
</example>

# Creating pull requests
Use the gh command via the Bash tool for ALL GitHub-related tasks including working with issues, pull requests, checks, and releases. If given a Github URL use the gh command to get the information needed.

1. Run the following bash commands in parallel using the Bash tool, in order to understand the current state of the branch since it diverged from the main branch:
   - Run a git status command to see all untracked files (never use -uall flag)
   - Run a git diff command to see both staged and unstaged changes that will be committed
   - Check if the current branch tracks a remote branch and is up to date with the remote, so you know if you need to push to the remote

   - Use the description/body for details, not the title

   - Create new branch if needed
   - Push to remote with -u flag if needed
   - Create PR using gh pr create with the format below. Use a HEREDOC to pass the body to ensure correct formatting. End the body with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.
<example>
gh pr create --title "the pr title" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'

<1-3 bullet points>

[Bulleted markdown checklist of TODOs for testing the pull request...]
EOF
)"
</example>

Important:

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem. You can access any file directly by using this tool.
Assume this tool is able to read all files on the machine. If the User provides a path to a file assume that path is valid. It is okay to read a file that does not exist; an error will be returned.

Usage:
- The file_path parameter must be an absolute path, not a relative path
- By default, it reads up to 2000 lines starting from the beginning of the file
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- This tool allows Claude Code to read images (eg PNG, JPG, etc). When reading an image file the contents are presented visually as Claude Code is a multimodal LLM.
- This tool can read PDF files (.pdf). For large PDFs (more than 10 pages), you MUST provide the pages parameter to read specific page ranges (e.g., pages: "1-5"). Reading a large PDF without the pages parameter will fail. Maximum 20 pages per request.
- This tool can read Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb files) and returns all cells with their outputs, combining code, text, and visualizations.
- This tool can only read files, not directories. To list files in a directory, use the registered shell tool.
- You will regularly be asked to read screenshots. If the user provides a path to a screenshot, ALWAYS use this tool to view the file at the path. This tool will work with all temporary file paths.
- If you read a file that exists but has empty contents you will receive a system reminder warning in place of file contents.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

1	# Native laboratory manual entry
2	
3	This is the first iOS app target for the existing Almanac core. It uses the
4	local package at `../Package.swift`; it adds no server, account system or
5	separately deployed service. The target supports iPhone and iPad on iOS 17+.
6	
7	## Authored
8	
9	- Reports: list, paginate, create, reopen, edit laboratory name and report date.
10	- Results: canonical/alias search, unmatched source names, create and edit.
11	- Numeric, qualitative, text, ratio, titer and absent values. Comparators,
12	  original units, original transcription, laboratory range text/bounds/units,
13	  reported flags, specimen, method, LOD/LOQ and derivation remain separate.
14	- Explicit date precision, including Unknown. No device date or timezone is
15	  filled into a historical result. Existing separately stored zone context
16	  survives a date edit; textual offsets take precedence in core date queries.
17	- Report detail, longitudinal test history with source-report navigation, and
18	  a separate revision history including metadata corrections and attribution.
19	- Incoming report-conflict review with explicit accept/reject and reason.
20	  There is no import automation creating these proposals in this app.
21	
22	The connection is owned on the main actor. Saving an existing result calls the
23	core's atomic value/metadata edit API. The application uses
24	`Application Support/Almanac/almanac.sqlite`, migrates in sequence, and seeds
25	idempotently. An open/migration failure displays an error; it never resets data.
26	The actor is `user` because this is the existing local personal database model,
27	not an authenticated multi-user service.
28	
29	## Verification boundary
30	
31	The Swift sources pass `swiftc -frontend -parse` on Linux. Project file
32	references and shared-scheme XML have been checked for internal consistency.
33	These are **syntax/structure checks, not Apple SDK compilation**.
34	
35	Not yet verified: SwiftUI type checking against an Apple SDK, Xcode package
36	resolution and linking, Simulator launch, interactive entry and navigation,
37	keyboard layout, accessibility, relaunch persistence through the app, device
38	signing or deployment. Linux core tests do not establish any of these.
39	
40	## Build and run on a Mac
41	
42	Open `Native/Almanac.xcodeproj`, select the shared `Almanac` scheme and an
43	installed iPhone Simulator, then Run. For a command-line Simulator build from
44	the repository root:
45	
46	```sh
47	xcodebuild -project Native/Almanac.xcodeproj -scheme Almanac \
48	  -configuration Debug -sdk iphonesimulator \
49	  -destination 'generic/platform=iOS Simulator' \
50	  CODE_SIGNING_ALLOWED=NO build
51	```
52	
53	The target has a provisional bundle identifier `com.almanac.personal`. Configure
54	a suitable identifier/team when preparing a physical-device build. This target
55	uses no HealthKit capability or document picker.
56	
57	## Interactive acceptance checks — outstanding
58	
59	1. Create a report with an unknown date; close and reopen the app and report.
60	2. Add Hemoglobin, HbA1c, Ferritin, Vitamin D, Creatinine and TSH through alias
61	   search. Copy original values, units and ranges from test fixtures or a
62	   report; do not infer a range. Add ANA with qualitative value `Negative`.
63	3. Add a bounded numeric result using `<`; verify both comparator and original
64	   transcription appear. Confirm a blank range remains “Not stated”.
65	4. Enter a month date, date-only, local time with no offset, Z timestamp and
66	   +03:00 timestamp. Save/reopen each without precision or timezone invention.
67	   Invalid calendar dates and offsets should display an error and leave data
68	   unchanged.
69	5. Edit one value A → B → A, supplying a reason each time. Revision history
70	   must show three events with only the latest current. Change only specimen
71	   or collection date and inspect the separate metadata correction record.
72	6. Add a second report with the same canonical test. Test history must show two
73	   measurements; their revision histories remain separate. Follow each source
74	   report link. Different units/specimens remain visible; no combined trend
75	   curve or unit conversion is inferred.
76	7. Clear an optional unit/range/date, save and reopen. Confirm the prior value
77	   is still accessible in history. Cancel an edit and confirm no save occurs.
78	8. Exercise compact/large Dynamic Type, VoiceOver, iPhone keyboard dismissal
79	   and iPad navigation. These interaction checks require the actual app.
80	
81	Report conflict behavior is covered in core tests. To exercise its UI, use a
82	development fixture that supplies conflicting reports via `upsertReport`; then
83	accept or reject with a reason and confirm the unresolved badge clears.
84	
85	Trends, document import, attachments, backup UI, OCR, medical interpretation,
86	and other tracker screens are outside this pass. The full earlier Laboratory
87	specification remains incomplete until the remaining features are implemented
88	and the real UI path above has been verified.

134	## 6. Shared measurement storage versus shared interfaces
135	
136	v0.1 said a shared measurement model is information-destroying. That was
137	wrong, and §13 records the correction. A shared model with enough dimensions —
138	value type, comparator, derivation, missing reason, source text, unit class,
139	precision — destroys nothing. What destroys information is an *under-specified*
140	shared model: a bare `value REAL` with an untyped `metadata JSON` beside it.
141	
142	So the real question is not "shared or specialised" but **what would a shared
143	model have to carry, and what does it cost to make every module pay for it.**
144	
145	| | One shared measurement table | Per-module tables |
146	|---|---|---|
147	| Dimensions | Must be the union of every module's: lab's five plus comparator plus ranges plus revision chain, nutrition's qualifier plus basis, exercise's type-dependent measured field. | Each module carries only its own. |
148	| Constraints | Table-level constraints must hold for every module, so most become nullable and unenforced; per-module validity moves into application code. | `CHECK` and `NOT NULL` express each module's real rules. |
149	| Foreign keys | Cannot point at module-specific parents (specimen, meal, bout) from one table without polymorphism. | Direct and enforced. |
150	| Aggregation | No shared aggregation is meaningful across modules anyway; every query re-adds module knowledge in its predicates. | Each module aggregates its own. |
151	| Schema change | A new module's dimension widens the shared table for all modules and rewrites one large table. | Additive, isolated. |
152	| Cross-module queries | Single table scan. | Requires a union or per-module queries. |
153	| Migration cost if reversed | Splitting a populated shared table per module is a data migration. | Merging later is also a data migration. |
154	
155	The deciding factor is not information loss. It is that the union of
156	dimensions is large, mostly nullable outside its own module, and unenforceable
157	at the table level — and the only benefit, one-table cross-module querying, is
158	addressed by §7 without a shared payload table.
159	
160	**Chosen: per-module tables, with shared behaviour expressed as protocols.**

164	## 7. The timeline — reassessment
165	
166	v0.1 proposed a persisted `health_event` index. This section reconsiders it
167	against the alternative of module-provided queries.
168	
169	**Module-provided queries:** each module implements a protocol returning its
170	own entries for a time range from its own tables; a thin coordinator merges the
171	results and orders them. No shared table, no second copy of anything.
172	
173	**Persisted event index:** each module also writes a row into a shared index
174	table; the coordinator queries that one table.
175	
176	| | Module-provided queries | Persisted event index |
177	|---|---|---|
178	| Second copy of data | None. | Yes — index rows duplicate identity and time. |
179	| Consistency risk | None. The module's record is the only copy. | Dual write; index can drift on insert, update, delete or revision. |
180	| Cross-module day view | N queries, merged in memory. | One indexed query. |
181	| Paging across long history | Needs an N-way merge cursor. | Natural. |
182	| Deletions and revisions | Automatic — the record is the truth. | Needs cascade rules and orphan repair. |
183	| New shared table names | None. | Occupies a generic name the unavailable spec may want (§12). |
184	| Cost to introduce later | Additive; buildable from module records at any time. | — |
185	| Cost to remove later | — | Modules already write to it; removal is a migration. |
186	
187	**Chosen: module-provided queries. The index is deferred.**
188	
189	*Implemented in exactly this form:* `TimelineProviding` on `LabStore` and
190	`HealthSampleStore`, merged by `Timeline` with a total order, and **no index
191	table**. See `docs/implementation-status.md` §2C.
192	
193	The concrete reason: the index's only genuine advantage is query performance
194	and paging ergonomics, and **there is no performance problem to solve** —
195	there are no modules, no data, no UI, and no measurement showing that an
196	N-way merge is too slow. Every other row favours the queries, and the
197	asymmetry is decisive: the index can be added later from module records
198	without changing a single module table, whereas removing it after modules
199	write to it is a data migration. Choosing the reversible option costs nothing
200	today.
201	
202	The trigger for revisiting, stated so the deferral is not indefinite: when a
203	range view must merge more than four modules, or page across more than a year
204	of history, **and** profiling shows the merge dominating.

263	## 8. Time, precision and zone
264	
265	Shared across every module. Laboratory §12 is the module-specific application.
266	
267	- Four distinct times, never interchangeable: **scheduled** (a plan's intended
268	  time), **occurrence** (when the thing happened — collection, meal, bout,
269	  sleep segment), **recording** (when it entered Almanac), and where a source
270	  issues records, **reported** (when the source issued it).
271	- Every stored time carries a **precision**: `instant` · `minute` · `hour` ·
272	  `day` · `month` · `year` · `unknown`.
273	- Every stored time carries an offset and, where known, a zone identifier, so
274	  a record made in another zone is not reinterpreted in the device's current
275	  one.
276	- **No timestamp is ever fabricated to fill a field.** A date-only fact stays
277	  at `day` precision.
278	
279	Day assignment:
280	
281	- Uses the occurrence time where present, else the reported time, else the
282	  recording time, and **records which was used**.
283	- Goes through `TimeModel` (`Time/TimeModel.swift`); no module formats a date.
284	- At `day` precision or coarser with a non-midnight boundary, the assignment
285	  is marked approximate. The boundary is still a placeholder
286	  (`TimeModel.swift:16-20`), so this case is currently the common one and must
287	  not be resolved by assuming a time.
288	
289	Interval overlap:
290	
291	- Defined only when both intervals have known start and end at `minute`
292	  precision or finer with known offsets.
293	- Otherwise the answer is **unknown**, which is a third value and not `false`.
294	  Sleep stage overlap, fasting windows and workout merging all depend on this.
295	
296	Ordering:
297	
298	- Records at `minute` precision or finer order against each other.
299	- Coarser records group as time-unknown within their day rather than sorting
300	  against an invented time.

305	
306	v0.1 conflated these. They are different mechanisms with different failure
307	modes.
308	
309	| | Import job | Sync cursor |
310	|---|---|---|
311	| Input | A document or file the user supplied. | A change stream the source exposes. |
312	| Identity | The document. | The stream position. |
313	| Progress record | Job row: status, counts, per-row outcomes, errors, document link. | Opaque anchor token per domain. |
314	| Re-running | Idempotent by source identity; produces the same rows. | Resumes from the anchor. |
315	| Failure | The job fails; the document remains; nothing is lost. | The anchor must not advance past unpersisted data. |

320	- **R9.1** File imports get their own job record. They do not use
321	  `sync_anchor`, and a cursor is not invented for them.

324	  call (`Sync/SyncAnchorStore.swift:44`), so advancing the anchor without
325	  persisting the rows it covers is expressible — and if it happened, the next

329	  advance together, so the unsafe ordering cannot be written.

333	  does not change; only the call shape does.

416	## 12. Does the missing Technical Spec create schema conflicts beyond numbering?
417	
418	Yes — three, all semantic rather than mechanical. None of them is a numbering
419	problem, and numbering is the least of them.
420	
421	1. **Duplicate definition of the same concept.** If the spec's 48 tables
422	   already define laboratory, sleep or timeline structures, building them now
423	   creates two homes for one fact. Reconciling that later is a data migration,
424	   not a rename.
425	2. **Name occupation.** A 48-table schema plausibly wants generic names —
426	   `event`, `observation`, `measurement`, `sample`, `source`, `document`. Any
427	   taken now forces the transcription to rename as it goes, and renaming
428	   during transcription is exactly where transcription errors enter.
429	3. **Contradicting invariants.** The spec defines the day-boundary rule, the
430	   readiness definition and the workout merge model. A module that hard-codes
431	   an assumption about any of them will disagree with the transcription
432	   silently rather than loudly.
433	
434	Mitigations, all cheap and all adopted by this proposal:
435	
436	- Prefix every new table with its module (`lab_*`). Claim no generic name.
437	- Introduce no new shared table at all — which §7 already concluded on other
438	  grounds, and which removes conflict class 2 for the timeline entirely.
439	- Hard-code no boundary, readiness or merge assumption; take them from
440	  injected configuration.
441	- Keep everything additive, so the transcription adds tables rather than
442	  reconciling them.
443	
444	One scoping observation worth stating: blood-test tracking entered Almanac's
445	scope on 2026-09-08, and the spec is dated 2026-08-05. It is therefore
446	**likely, though unverified, that Laboratory is not among the 48 tables** — in
447	which case conflict class 1 does not apply to this module. That is a
448	probability, not a finding, and it is listed as an open question in §15.

## Summary of findings

### 1. `Native/Almanac.xcodeproj` and everything under `Native/`

Full file listing under `Native/`:

```
Native/Almanac.xcodeproj/project.pbxproj
Native/Almanac.xcodeproj/xcshareddata/xcschemes/Almanac.xcscheme
Native/Almanac/AlmanacApp.swift
Native/Almanac/HistoryViews.swift
Native/Almanac/ReportViews.swift
Native/Almanac/ResultEditor.swift
Native/README.md
```

- **`project.pbxproj`** — a real, hand-authored (not Xcode-generated-looking, but valid) project file. Objects use `objectVersion = 56`, `LastUpgradeCheck = 1500`. One target: `Almanac` (`productType = com.apple.product-type.application`), product `Almanac.app`. It references the four `.swift` files above (all in group `Almanac`), a `PBXFrameworksBuildPhase` linking one Swift package product dependency (`AlmanacCore`), and an `XCLocalSwiftPackageReference` with `relativePath = ..` — i.e. it consumes the **local** `AlmanacCore` package one directory up (the repo's `Package.swift`), not a remote/pinned dependency.
  - Build settings of note: `IPHONEOS_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET = 17.0`, `SDKROOT = iphoneos`, `SUPPORTED_PLATFORMS = "iphoneos iphonesimulator"`, `SUPPORTS_MACCATALYST = NO`, `TARGETED_DEVICE_FAMILY = "1,2"` (iPhone+iPad), `SWIFT_VERSION = 5.0`, `CODE_SIGN_STYLE = Automatic`, `PRODUCT_BUNDLE_IDENTIFIER = com.almanac.personal` (provisional), `MARKETING_VERSION = 0.1.0`.
  - **`GENERATE_INFOPLIST_FILE = YES`** — there is **no physical `Info.plist` file**; Xcode auto-generates it from `INFOPLIST_KEY_*` build settings. Present keys: `INFOPLIST_KEY_CFBundleDisplayName = Almanac`, `INFOPLIST_KEY_UIApplicationSceneManifest_Generation = YES`, `INFOPLIST_KEY_UILaunchScreen_Generation = YES`, `INFOPLIST_KEY_UISupportedInterfaceOrientations = "...Portrait LandscapeLeft LandscapeRight"`. **No HealthKit usage-description keys** (`NSHealthShareUsageDescription`/`NSHealthUpdateUsageDescription`) and **no notification-related keys** are present anywhere.
  - **No entitlements file** exists or is referenced (no `CODE_SIGN_ENTITLEMENTS` setting) — so no HealthKit capability, no push/notification capability is wired up yet.
  - **No storyboards** — this is a pure SwiftUI app (`@main` `App` struct, `WindowGroup`), no `UIApplicationDelegate`/`SceneDelegate`/storyboard files at all.
- **`Almanac.xcscheme`** — one shared scheme named `Almanac`, straightforward build/test/launch/profile/analyze/archive actions all pointed at the single `Almanac` target. Nothing unusual.
- **Four Swift source files**, all SwiftUI, all `import AlmanacCore`:
  - `AlmanacApp.swift` — `@main` `AlmanacApp: App`, plus `LaboratoryModel: ObservableObject` (`@MainActor`) that owns the `Database`/`LabStore`/`LabCatalogStore`, opens the SQLite file at `Application Support/Almanac/almanac.sqlite`, runs migrations, seeds the catalog. Also has shared helpers: `EditorFailure`, `optionalText`, `dateLabel`, `readable`, an `View.editorError(_:)` alert modifier, and `PartialDateFields`/`editedDate` for the app's explicit-precision date entry pattern.
  - `ReportViews.swift` — `ReportListView`, `ReportEditor`, `ReportDetailView` (list/create/edit lab reports).
  - `ResultEditor.swift` — `ResultEditor` (add/edit a single lab result: value type, comparator, specimen, ranges, catalog search, etc.).
  - `HistoryViews.swift` — `ResultSummary`, `ContentDetails`, `MeasurementHistoryView`, `RevisionHistoryView`, `ReportConflictView`.
  - All of this is the **Laboratory / manual lab-entry** feature only. There is nothing hydration-, dashboard-, settings-, HealthKit-, or notification-related in `Native/` today.
- **`Native/README.md`** states explicitly: *"This target uses no HealthKit capability or document picker,"* gives the `xcodebuild` command for a simulator build, and lists interactive acceptance checks still outstanding (never run on an Apple platform — only `swiftc -frontend -parse` on Linux has verified these files).

### 2. Existing SwiftUI code anywhere in the repo

Only in `Native/Almanac/*.swift` (the four files above — `import SwiftUI` appears in `AlmanacApp.swift`, `HistoryViews.swift`, `ReportViews.swift`, `ResultEditor.swift`). No SwiftUI code exists in `Sources/AlmanacCore` (by design — it's a cross-platform Linux/macOS-buildable package with zero Apple framework imports) or anywhere else in the repo.

### 3. Existing HealthKit code

No `import HealthKit`, `HKHealthStore`, or `HKQuantityType` usage exists anywhere yet. What exists is a **protocol seam** for it:
- `Sources/AlmanacCore/Health/HealthProvider.swift` — defines `protocol HealthProvider` (`requestAuthorisation(for:)`, `changes(in:since:)`), `enum HealthDomain` (currently `sleep, workouts, activeEnergy, restingEnergy, steps, heartRate, hrv, bodyMass` — **no hydration/water domain yet**), `HealthSample`, `HealthChangeSet`, `HealthProviderError`, and an in-memory `FakeHealthProvider` used by tests. Doc comments explicitly say: *"The concrete `HealthKitProvider` belongs in the iOS target and is the only place `import HealthKit` may appear."*
- `Sources/AlmanacCore/Health/HealthSampleStore.swift` and `Sources/AlmanacCore/Health/HealthSyncService.swift` — persistence/sync logic built against the `HealthProvider` protocol (tested via `FakeHealthProvider`, see `Tests/AlmanacCoreTests/HealthSyncTests.swift`).
- No concrete `HealthKitProvider` iOS adapter exists in `Native/` yet — that's still to be written, per both `Native/README.md` and `docs/architecture/health-data-foundation.md`.

### 4. Existing local-notification code

None found. No matches for `UNUserNotificationCenter` or `UNNotificationRequest` anywhere in the repo.

### 5. `Package.swift`

```swift
// swift-tools-version:5.9
let package = Package(
    name: "AlmanacCore",
    platforms: [.iOS(.v17), .macOS(.v14)],
    products: [
        .library(name: "AlmanacCore", targets: ["AlmanacCore"])
    ],
    targets: [
        .target(name: "CSQLite", path: "Sources/CSQLite", sources: ["sqlite3.c"], ...),
        .target(name: "AlmanacCore", dependencies: ["CSQLite"], path: "Sources/AlmanacCore"),
        .testTarget(name: "AlmanacCoreTests", dependencies: ["AlmanacCore"], path: "Tests/AlmanacCoreTests")
    ]
)
```
- Platform minimums: **iOS 17, macOS 14**.
- Only **library** and **test** targets — `.library(name: "AlmanacCore", ...)`, plus the vendored `CSQLite` C target and `AlmanacCoreTests`. **No executable/app target is defined in `Package.swift`** — the app target lives entirely in `Native/Almanac.xcodeproj` and consumes this package as a local SwiftPM dependency (per the `XCLocalSwiftPackageReference` noted above), not via a Package.swift executable/iOS-app product (SwiftPM doesn't produce `.app` bundles anyway).

### 6. README / docs / implementation-status

- `README.md` (root) — describes `AlmanacCore` as "the platform-free half of Slice 1 — Foundation," a status table (DatabaseManager, migration runner, TimeModel, HealthProvider seam, SyncAnchor, BackupService, provenance enums all "Built"; the 48-table domain schema explicitly "NOT BUILT — spec unavailable"). Notably: *"The iOS app target imports this package, and `import HealthKit` may appear in exactly one file there: the concrete `HealthProvider`."*
- `docs/implementation-status.md` (current, updated 2026-09-13) — the authoritative up-to-date status doc. Key points:
  - Verified: 115 Swift tests pass on Linux (Swift 6.3.3), 101 Python tests for the nutrition tooling. **No change has ever been run on an Apple platform.**
  - "Interface status" section: confirms `Native/Almanac` + `Native/Almanac.xcodeproj` is the only native app work; lists implemented screens (report list/create/edit/detail, result entry/editing, test history, revision history, report-conflict resolution) — all Laboratory-only.
  - "Remaining boundaries": Apple SDK compilation/Simulator launch/interactive UI verification not yet performed; no multi-user/account layer; "no automatic unit conversion, OCR, AI interpretation, or new tracker."
  - Nutrition section: bundle import into the app target and food logging/portions explicitly **not done yet** ("blocked on Yazeed" for dish data, "needs the Apple toolchain" for app wiring).
- Earlier status commit `6cbd49e` ("Update implementation status for the correctness pass", 2026-09-08) has a detailed **"§4b. The native manual-entry flow — smallest next step"** section that is highly relevant to planning a new app target:
  - Confirms **a Mac is required** to build/sign — no supported way to build iOS apps on Linux; this was called "the blocker."
  - Table of requirements for adding an app target: Xcode+iOS SDK (covered since package already targets `.iOS(.v17)`), a new App target (none existed at that point — this is what became `Native/Almanac.xcodeproj`), bundle ID + signing team, **HealthKit capability/entitlement + the two Info.plist usage strings explicitly deferred out of the first pass** ("deliberately... the first app target can skip the entitlement entirely and stay simple"), and the SQLite database location in Application Support.
  - Explicitly states the first app target's scope was: "One SwiftUI target, no HealthKit, no import, no documents, no timeline screen" — four Laboratory views only. This scope was realized as-is in the current `Native/Almanac.xcodeproj`.
- `docs/architecture/health-data-foundation.md` (v0.2, "proposal" status, not yet applied to code) — the shared cross-module architecture doc. Highly relevant background for a hydration feature:
  - Decision: **per-module tables**, not a shared "measurement" table; shared behavior via protocols (`TimelineProviding`).
  - Decision: **no persisted timeline/event index** — each module implements `TimelineProviding` (`entries(from:to:in:) -> [TimelineEntry]`) and a coordinator merges results in memory; this is already implemented for `LabStore`/`HealthSampleStore` via `Timeline`.
  - §8: time/precision/zone rules apply to every module — four distinct time kinds (scheduled/occurrence/recording/reported), explicit `TimePrecision`, no fabricated timestamps.
  - §9: import jobs vs. sync cursors are different mechanisms; sync-cursor advance and row writes must commit in one transaction (a stated but *not yet implemented* requirement on `SyncAnchorStore`).
  - §10: identity rules — surrogate IDs, source-scoped external IDs, revision chains, no silent merging — apply equally to HealthKit-sourced data.
  - §11: migration numbering is **not yet frozen** in general, but *is* effectively committed for existing modules (current migrations run through 011 per `Sources/AlmanacCore/Persistence/Migration011.swift`); a new hydration module would add new migrations "002 upward" style, using its own `hydration_*`-prefixed tables (per §12's rule: "Prefix every new table with its module... Claim no generic name").
  - §15 "Needs Yazeed": open product questions including document storage model, interpretation boundary, etc. — worth checking before building.
- `docs/features/laboratory.md`, `docs/features/nutrition.md`, `docs/features/laboratory-catalog-coverage.md` exist but are Laboratory/Nutrition-specific; **no hydration feature doc exists in the repo at all** — a grep for "hydration" across the whole repo only turns up unrelated nutrition dictionary/energy-estimate hits (e.g. hydration-related nutrient names in `tools/nutrition/dictionary/nutrients.csv`, `GeneralAtwaterTests.swift`), not a hydration tracking feature.

### 7. CI configuration

**No `.github/` directory exists in the repo at all** (`.github/workflows` not found), and no other CI config (`.gitlab-ci.yml`, `.circleci/`, etc.) was found — a repo-wide search for `*.yml`/`*.yaml` outside `.build/` found nothing. So there is currently **no CI pipeline** constraining how an app target should be added; all verification described in the docs (Linux `swift build`/`swift test`, `swiftc -frontend -parse` for the Native Swift files) has been run manually by the assistant/user, not via automated CI. `env.sh` (repo root) is the manual toolchain setup script (`source env.sh` puts Swift 6.3.3 and vendored `libxml2`/ICU deps on `PATH`/`LD_LIBRARY_PATH`) referenced throughout the docs.

---

**Net takeaway for planning:** The `Native/Almanac.xcodeproj` app target is real, minimal, and currently scoped strictly to the Laboratory feature — one target, four SwiftUI files, no Info.plist file (generated from build settings), no entitlements, no HealthKit, no notifications, no CI. Adding `HydrationLoggingView`, `HydrationDashboardView`, `SettingsView`, a `HydrationLoggingService`, HealthKit integration, and local notifications will require: (1) new Swift files added to the existing target (and to `project.pbxproj`'s `PBXGroup`/`PBXBuildFile`/`PBXSourcesBuildPhase` entries, or regenerating the project), (2) a `CODE_SIGN_ENTITLEMENTS` file + `com.apple.developer.healthkit` entitlement + the two `NSHealthShareUsageDescription`/`NSHealthUpdateUsageDescription` `INFOPLIST_KEY_*` settings (or a real `Info.plist`) for HealthKit, (3) a `NSUserNotificationsUsageDescription`/local-notification authorization request (no Info.plist key strictly required for local notifications, but authorization must be requested at runtime), (4) a concrete `HealthKitProvider: HealthProvider` in the iOS target per the existing seam in `Sources/AlmanacCore/Health/HealthProvider.swift` (likely needs a new `.hydration`/`.water` case added to `HealthDomain`), (5) a new `hydration_*`-prefixed migration/table set in `AlmanacCore` following the module-owns-its-tables + `TimelineProviding` pattern already established for Laboratory/Health, and (6) since there's no CI, no automated gate will catch build breaks — verification stays manual (`swiftc -frontend -parse` on Linux for syntax, real Xcode/Simulator build on a Mac for everything else), consistent with how the existing Laboratory UI was built and documented as unverified on Apple platforms.
